questions.question: What invariant makes an image vector directly comparable with a text vector in CLIP?
options: Both encoders must use the same Transformer weights.
Both outputs are projected to the same dimension and L2-normalized before similarity.
Every text must contain the image filename.
Both modalities must have the same number of input tokens.
questions.explanation: The towers can have different architectures and widths. Paired projections plus normalization create the common geometry used by the dot product.

questions.question: A global training batch contains N paired examples. How many candidate negatives does one image row receive under the standard in-batch objective?
options: N squared
One
Two times N
N minus 1
questions.explanation: The diagonal text is the declared positive for that image; the other N - 1 texts in the row act as candidate negatives.

questions.question: Why can a larger batch harm learning when the dataset contains near-duplicate images and alternative valid captions?
options: It can label more semantically valid off-diagonal pairs as negatives.
It removes the image-to-text loss.
It prevents embedding normalization.
It forces both towers to share weights.
questions.explanation: More in-batch candidates increase useful hard negatives and the chance of false negatives. Pair identity and duplicate handling are therefore part of data quality.

questions.question: What happens when logit scale becomes very large while cosine geometry and labels stay fixed?
options: The image resolution increases.
The tokenizer vocabulary expands.
Softmax becomes sharper, so small similarity differences and mislabeled pairs receive more confident penalties.
The embedding dimension becomes smaller.
questions.explanation: Logit scale changes how strongly softmax responds to similarity gaps. It cannot repair bad geometry or noisy pair labels.

questions.question: A new image processor emits the same tensor shape but uses a different crop policy. What is the correct release treatment?
options: Approve it because the model endpoint remains available.
Treat it as contract drift, run golden fixtures and slice evaluation, and rebuild image-derived artifacts if approved.
Change only the text prompt bank.
Skip evaluation because embedding dimension did not change.
questions.explanation: Shape compatibility does not preserve semantic geometry. Crop policy is part of the image contract and can alter every catalog vector.

questions.question: Why must a retrieval release rebuild or verify the catalog index when the image tower changes?
options: Stored image vectors were produced in the previous model geometry and may no longer be comparable with new text vectors.
Approximate search requires raw image pixels in every query.
The tokenizer cannot run until the index is rebuilt.
Recall@K is defined only for fresh images.
questions.explanation: A vector index is versioned derived data. Mixing vectors from different image and text manifests can silently corrupt ranking even when dimensions match.

questions.question: Which evaluation portfolio best supports a zero-shot classifier that can receive out-of-domain inputs?
options: Training loss and image-encoder throughput only
One aggregate top-1 score using one prompt
Retrieval Recall@10 without class labels
Per-class and slice metrics, prompt comparisons, calibration, and an unknown or abstain test
questions.explanation: The product decision depends on class coverage, wording, calibration, and behavior when no offered class is correct, not only aggregate accuracy.

questions.question: A quantized bundle cuts p95 latency in half but fails a declared language slice. What should the release gate do?
options: Promote it because latency improved.
Average the slice with the strongest class.
Hold or narrow the release until the blocking slice has passing evidence.
Increase logit scale to hide the regression.
questions.explanation: Independent release gates prevent operational wins from numerically offsetting a protected-slice failure.
